But we do not have the algebraic rule defining the integrand $$c$$ for all values of $$t$$ in $$\lbrack 0,28\rbrack$$ . In fact, we are given its values only at a set of discrete points in that interval. In situations such as this, the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus proves useless because we cannot find an antiderivative of $$c$$ . (We will complete the solution to this problem in Example 4.)

Other situations also arise in which an integrable function has an antiderivative that cannot be found in terms of elementary functions (functions that can be expressed as a finite combination of algebraic, exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions). Examples of such functions are

Riemann sums provide us with a good approximation of a definite integral, provided that the number of subintervals in the partitions is large enough. But there are better techniques and formulas, called quadrature formulas, that give a more efficient way of computing approximate values of definite integrals. In this section, we look at two rather simple but effective ways of approximating definite integrals.

subsection.title: The Trapezoidal Rule
subsection.paragraph: We assume that $$f(x) \geq 0$$ on $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ to simplify the derivation of the Trapezoidal Rule, but the result is valid without this restriction. We begin by subdividing the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ into $$n$$ subintervals of equal length $$\Delta x$$ , by means of the $$\left( {n + 1} \right)$$ points $$x_{0} = a,x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n} = b$$ , where $$n$$ is a positive integer (Figure 3).

Furthermore, as we saw earlier, we may view the definite integral

as the area of the region $$R$$ under the curve $$y = f(x)$$ between $$x = a$$ and $$x = b$$ . This area is given by the sum of the areas of the $$n$$ nonoverlapping subregions $$R_{1},R_{2},\ldots,R_{n}$$ , where $$R_{1}$$ represents the region under the curve $$y = f(x)$$ from $$x = x_{0}$$ to $$x = x_{1}$$ , and so on.

The basis for the Trapezoidal Rule lies in the approximation of each region, $$R_{1},R_{2},\ldots,R_{n}$$ by a suitable trapezoid. This often leads to a much better approximation than one obtained by means of rectangles (a Riemann sum).

Let’s consider the subregion $$R_{1}$$ , shown magnified for the sake of clarity in Figure 4. Observe that the area of the region $$R_{1}$$ may be approximated by the trapezoid of width $$\Delta x$$ whose parallel sides are of lengths $$f\left( x_{0} \right)$$ and $$f\left( x_{1} \right)$$ . subsection.title: Simpson’s Rule
subsection.paragraph: Before stating Simpson’s Rule, let’s review the two rules we have used in approximating a definite integral. Let $$f$$ be a continuous, nonnegative function defined on the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ . Suppose the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ is partitioned by means of the $$n + 1$$ equally spaced points $$x_{0} = a,x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n} = b$$ where $$n$$ is a positive integer, so that the length of each subinterval is $$\Delta x = {\left( {b - a} \right) \slash n}$$ (Figure 5).

The region below the curve is segmented by the perpendiculars dropped from the path of the curve to the tick marks x_0, x_1, x_2, x_3, x_n minus 1, and x_n each in the x axis. The region between the tick marks a = x_0 and x_1 is labeled R_1, x_1 and x_2 is labeled R_2, x_2 and x_3 labeled is R_3, x_n minus 1 and x_n = b is labeled R_n.

subsection.paragraph: Let’s concentrate on the portion of the graph of $$y = f(x)$$ defined on the interval $$\left\lbrack {x_{0},x_{2}} \right\rbrack$$ . When we use a Riemann sum to approximate the definite integral, we are in effect approximating the function $$f(x)$$ on $$\left\lbrack {x_{0},x_{1}} \right\rbrack$$ by the constant function $$y = f\left( p_{1} \right)$$ , where $$p_{1}$$ is chosen to be a point in $$\left\lbrack {x_{0},x_{1}} \right\rbrack$$ ; and we are approximating the function $$f(x)$$ on $$\left\lbrack {x_{1},x_{2}} \right\rbrack$$ by the constant function $$y = f\left( p_{2} \right)$$ , where $$p_{2}$$ lies in $$\left\lbrack {x_{1},x_{2}} \right\rbrack$$ . Using a Riemann sum, we see that the area of the region under the curve $$y = f(x)$$ between $$x = x_{0}$$ and $$x = x_{2}$$ is approximated by the area of the region under the approximating “step” function (Figure 6a).

The region enclosed by the trapezoids is shaded.

subsection.paragraph: When we use the Trapezoidal Rule, we are in effect approximating the function $$f(x)$$ on the interval $$\left\lbrack {x_{0},x_{1}} \right\rbrack$$ by a linear function through the two points $$\left( {x_{0},f\left( x_{0} \right)} \right)$$ and $$\left( {x_{1},f\left( x_{1} \right)} \right)$$ and the function $$f(x)$$ on $$\left\lbrack {x_{1},x_{2}} \right\rbrack$$ by a linear function through the two points $$\left( {x_{1},f\left( x_{1} \right)} \right)$$ and $$\left( {x_{2},f\left( x_{2} \right)} \right)$$ . Thus, the Trapezoidal Rule simply approximates the actual area of the region under the curve $$y = f(x)$$ from $$x = x_{0}$$ to $$x = x_{2}$$ by the area of the region under the approximating polygonal curve (Figure 6b).

A natural extension of the preceding idea is to approximate portions of the graph of $$y = f(x)$$ by means of portions of the graphs of second-degree polynomials (parts of parabolas). It can be shown that given any three noncollinear points, there is a unique parabola that passes through the given points. Choose the points $$\left( {x_{0},f\left( x_{0} \right)} \right)$$ , $$\left( {x_{1},f\left( x_{1} \right)} \right)$$ , and $$\left( {x_{2},f\left( x_{2} \right)} \right)$$ corresponding to the first three points of the partition. Then we can approximate the function $$f(x)$$ on $$\left\lbrack {x_{0},x_{2}} \right\rbrack$$ by means of a quadratic function whose graph contains these three points (Figure 7).

statement.paragraph: In using the Trapezoidal Rule, the number of subintervals $$n$$ must be even.
In using Simpson’s Rule, the number of subintervals $$n$$ may be chosen to be odd or even.
Simpson’s Rule is more accurate than the Trapezoidal Rule.
If $$f$$ is a polynomial function of degree less than or equal to $$3$$ , then the approximation of $$\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)dx}$$ using Simpson’s Rule is exact.
Derive the formula

for calculating the cardiac output of a person in liters per minute. Here, $$c(t)$$ is the concentration of dye in the aorta (in milligrams per liter) at time $$t$$ (in seconds) for $$t$$ in $$\left\lbrack {0,T} \right\rbrack$$ , and $$D$$ is the amount of dye (in milligrams) injected into a vein leading to the heart.

Hint: Partition the interval $$\left\lbrack {0,T} \right\rbrack$$ into $$n$$ subintervals of equal length $$\Delta t$$ . The amount of dye that flows past the measuring point in the aorta during the time interval $$\left\lbrack {0,\Delta t} \right\rbrack$$ is approximately $${c\left( t_{i} \right)\left( {R\Delta t} \right)} \slash 60$$ (concentration times volume). Therefore, the total amount of dye measured at the aorta is

paragraph.math: $$\frac{\left\lbrack {c\left( t_{1} \right)R\Delta t + c\left( t_{2} \right)R\Delta t + \cdots + c\left( t_{n} \right)R\Delta t} \right\rbrack}{60} = D$$
